# 1. serde conventions for stable wire formats

## 1a. `snake_case` vs `camelCase` — what comparable crates actually pick

Surveyed by reading actual source. **The split is clean and it is not about taste — it is about lineage:**

| Crate | Casing | Evidence |
| :-- | :-- | :-- |
| `oci-spec-rs` | `camelCase` (~50), `SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE` (7, for `LinuxCapability`/`Signal`), `PascalCase` (1, Docker-legacy `Config`) | `src/image/descriptor.rs:8-11` |
| `lsp-types` | `camelCase` × **289**, `lowercase` × 10 | `src/lib.rs:947` |
| `cargo_metadata` | **no `rename_all` on any struct** — Rust `snake_case` passes through, because cargo's JSON *is* snake_case | `src/lib.rs:257` |
| `rustc --error-format=json` | `snake_case` (`byte_start`, `suggested_replacement`) plus sigil `$message_type` | [rustc json.md](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustc/json.html) |
| `scip` (protobuf) | ProtoJSON mandates lowerCamelCase; the Rust bindings contain **zero serde** | `bindings/rust/Cargo.toml` |
| `serde-sarif` | `camelCase` (generated from the OASIS JSON Schema) | `serde-sarif/src/sarif.rs:21` |

```rust
// containers/oci-spec-rs @ src/image/descriptor.rs:8-11 — the ENTIRE container attr set
#[derive(Builder, Clone, CopyGetters, Debug, Deserialize, Eq, Getters, Setters, PartialEq, Serialize)]
#[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")]
```

**Is there documented reason?** No. serde takes no position — [serde.rs/container-attrs.html](https://serde.rs/container-attrs.html) just enumerates the eight legal values. The [Rust API Guidelines](https://rust-lang.github.io/api-guidelines/) say nothing about JSON casing. The only *normative* citations are external-spec ones:

- [protobuf.dev/programming-guides/json](https://protobuf.dev/programming-guides/json/): *"Message field names are mapped to lowerCamelCase to be used as JSON object keys."*
- [google.aip.dev/140](https://google.aip.dev/140): *"Field definitions in protobuf files **must** use `lower_snake_case` names"* — i.e. declare snake, emit camel, mechanically.

**Rule the evidence supports:** if Wisp's JSON is Rust-tooling-native (produced and consumed by your four repos, not mirroring an external spec), **`snake_case` with no `rename_all` at all** is the majority precedent and eliminates a whole class of rename drift — you cannot get a casing bug in a field you never renamed. Only reach for `camelCase` if the MCP/JS side is a first-class consumer where camel is the house style. Whichever you pick, deviate only where a spec forces it, the way oci-spec-rs does:

```rust
// oci-spec-rs src/image/config.rs:69 — spec-literal names override the convention, don't bend it
#[serde(rename = "os.version", skip_serializing_if = "Option::is_none")]
os_version: Option<String>,
```

## 1b. `deny_unknown_fields` — the precise forward-compat tradeoff

**Census across the surveyed crates: `deny_unknown_fields` appears ZERO times.** Not in oci-spec-rs, not in lsp-types (289 wire structs), not in cargo_metadata, not in serde-sarif — and serde-sarif's bundled schema contains **52 instances of `"additionalProperties": false`**, i.e. even a format that officially declares itself closed gets a Rust deserializer that shrugs at unknown fields.

serde's own doc, [container-attrs.html](https://serde.rs/container-attrs.html):

> Always error during deserialization when encountering unknown fields. When this attribute is not present, **by default unknown fields are ignored for self-describing formats like JSON.**

**The tradeoff stated precisely:** `deny_unknown_fields` converts *"a newer producer emitted a field I don't know about"* from a no-op into a **hard deserialization failure of the entire document**. There is no partial recovery — you lose the fields you *do* understand. In a four-repo polyrepo this means: the moment repo A ships `wisp-contracts` v1.1 with a new field and starts emitting it, every repo still on v1.0 **stops working**, and the failure is total, not degraded. You have converted an additive change into a lockstep-deploy requirement across four repos.

Real production incident report: [aws-lambda-rust-runtime#750](https://github.com/aws/aws-lambda-rust-runtime/issues/750):

> If the Amazon API Gateway team were to add a new feature that involved a new request field, all deployed Rust Lambda functions using the Lambda proxy integration might immediately break in production. In most APIs, adding a new field is not considered a breaking change.

**The accepted rule: deny on config, allow on wire.** Config files are authored by a human who benefits enormously from `unknown field "tiemout"` instead of silent misconfiguration, and there is no forward-compat requirement because the config and the binary ship together. Wire types are the opposite on both counts.

**Do not rely on the tolerance being accidental** — [RFC 9413 "Maintaining Robust Protocols"](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9413.html) argues leniency-by-default is not an extensibility strategy. Specify it. rustc's one sentence is the model to copy verbatim into your contract doc:

> Optional values may be `null`. New fields may be added. Enumerated fields like "level" or "suggestion_applicability" may add new values.

And the [cargo registry API](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/registry-web-api.html) version:

> For backwards compatibility, servers should ignore any unexpected query parameters or JSON fields. If a JSON field is missing, it should be assumed to be null.

**One caveat for schemars:** `#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]` is *read by schemars* and emits `"additionalProperties": false`. Verified:

```
Strict schema = {"$schema":"https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema","title":"Strict",
  "type":"object","properties":{"a":{...}},"additionalProperties":false,"required":["a"]}
```

That published `false` is then a promise to every MCP client, and [JSON Schema's own docs](https://json-schema.org/understanding-json-schema/reference/object) flag it as an obstacle to extension: *"`additionalProperties` only recognizes properties declared in the same subschema as itself... `additionalProperties` can restrict you from 'extending' a schema using combining keywords such as `allOf`."* So the attribute costs you twice — once in Rust, once in the published contract.

## 1c. Tagging representations: what works with what

From [serde.rs/enum-representations.html](https://serde.rs/enum-representations.html), all four claims below confirmed empirically.

| | Externally tagged (default) | Internally `tag="k"` | Adjacently `tag,content` | Untagged |
| :-- | :-- | :-- | :-- | :-- |
| Tuple variants | ✅ | ❌ **compile error** | ✅ | ✅ |
| Newtype-of-primitive | ✅ | ❌ **runtime error** | ✅ | ✅ |
| Non-self-describing formats | ✅ **only one** | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ |
| Needs `alloc` to deserialize | no | **yes** | **yes** | **yes** |
| Works with `#[serde(other)]` | ✅ (undocumented, see below) | ✅ | ✅ | n/a |
| Works with `flatten` | — | — | — | — (see 1c-flatten) |

serde's doc, verbatim:

> This representation works for struct variants, newtype variants containing structs or maps, and unit variants but **does not work for enums containing tuple variants. Using a `#[serde(tag = "...")]` attribute on an enum containing a tuple variant is an error at compile time.**

> All enum representations work in no-std projects, but **externally tagged is the only one that works in no-alloc projects.**

**Newtype-of-primitive — this compiles fine and blows up at runtime.** This is the trap:

```rust
#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize, Debug)]
#[serde(tag = "kind", rename_all = "snake_case")]
enum Bad { Num(u32), Obj(Inner) }   // compiles!
```
```
Bad::Obj = Ok("{\"kind\":\"obj\",\"x\":1}")
Bad::Num = Err(Error("cannot serialize tagged newtype variant Bad::Num containing an integer", line: 0, column: 0))
```
The error text is generated at [`serde/src/private/ser.rs:87`](https://github.com/serde-rs/serde/blob/master/serde/src/private/ser.rs). For a stable wire format this is the worst failure class you can ship: a type that type-checks, passes a partial test suite, and fails only on the variant nobody exercised.

**Non-self-describing formats — buffering, demonstrated.** Internally- and adjacently-tagged deserialization buffers the input into serde's private `Content` enum and requires `deserialize_any`. Verified against `postcard` 1.x:

```
internal ser bytes = [1, 97, 7]                                     // serializes fine!
internal de = Err("This is a feature that PostCard will never implement")
external de = Ok(A { x: 7 })                                        // only this works
adjacent de = Err("This is a feature that PostCard will never implement")
```

Note the asymmetry — **serialization succeeds, deserialization fails.** If you ever want a compact binary sidecar (postcard/bincode/CBOR-canonical) for the same vocabulary types, internally-tagged is a one-way door. The buffering also costs you zero-copy: a buffered `Content` cannot yield borrowed `&'de str`, so `#[serde(borrow)]` is dead inside a tagged enum, and there is a measurable allocation per value.

**`flatten` + `deny_unknown_fields`.** The doc says flatly ([field-attrs](https://serde.rs/field-attrs.html)):

> Note: this attribute is not supported in combination with structs that use `deny_unknown_fields`. Neither the outer nor inner flattened struct should use that attribute.

Reality in 1.0.229 is worse than a compile error — **it compiles, and silently does the wrong thing.** Verified:

```rust
#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize, Debug)]
#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]
struct WithMap { a: u32, #[serde(flatten)] rest: BTreeMap<String, serde_json::Value> }
```
```
map  Err("unknown field `z` at line 1 column 13")   // the catch-all map catches NOTHING
both Ok(OuterStrictInner { a: 1, rest: InnerStrict { b: 2 } })  // this case happens to work
```
The catch-all map rejects exactly the keys it exists to absorb. Tracked in [serde#2384](https://github.com/serde-rs/serde/issues/2384) ("works at least in simple cases", docs say otherwise), [serde#2283](https://github.com/serde-rs/serde/issues/2283) ("`flatten` bypasses the `deny_unknown_fields` check"), [serde#1600](https://github.com/serde-rs/serde/issues/1600), [serde#2634](https://github.com/serde-rs/serde/issues/2634) ("deny_unknown_fields docs misleading"). Also relevant: [serde#2121](https://github.com/serde-rs/serde/issues/2121) — `deny_unknown_fields` + `skip` is also broken (a skipped field produces `unknown field`).

**Recommendation for Wisp:** adjacently tagged (`tag="kind", content="data"`) if you need to carry tuple or primitive payloads and want to keep the binary-format door open on the *serialize* side; internally tagged (`tag="kind"`) only if every variant is a struct variant or a struct-shaped newtype, which is the more readable JSON and what `cargo_metadata`'s `Message` uses. Never untagged for a versioned wire format — serde tries variants in order and the first success wins, so adding a variant can silently reroute existing documents, and the error on total failure is famously uninformative (serde's own docs recommend `#[serde(expecting = "...")]` to patch this).

## 1d. `#[non_exhaustive]` — exactly what it costs downstream

Verified with a real two-crate workspace (defining crate `voc`, consumer `down`). **Within the defining crate `#[non_exhaustive]` has no effect at all** — which is precisely why serde's derive is unaffected.

**On a struct** — three distinct errors, all from `down`:

```rust
let _m  = Meta { id: "x".into(), n: 1 };        // error[E0639]: cannot create non-exhaustive struct using struct expression
let _m2 = Meta { n: 2, ..Default::default() };  // error[E0639]: cannot create non-exhaustive struct using struct expression
let Meta { id: _, n: _ } = m3;                  // error[E0638]: `..` required with struct marked as non-exhaustive
```

So yes: struct-literal construction, **functional update syntax `..Default::default()`**, and exhaustive destructuring are all blocked. `..` in a pattern fixes the third; the first two require you to ship a constructor and/or `Default`.

**On an enum:**

```
error[E0004]: non-exhaustive patterns: `_` not covered
   = note: `Kind` is marked as non-exhaustive, so a wildcard `_` is necessary to match exhaustively
```

**The `as`-cast rule in the cargo semver reference is imprecise — I verified the distinction.** The reference says flatly *"Casting enum variants to their discriminant with `as` is not allowed."* In fact:

```rust
#[non_exhaustive] pub enum EnumLevel { A = 1, B = 2 }          // enum-level
pub enum VariantLevel { #[non_exhaustive] First = 1, Second = 2 }  // variant-level
```
```rust
let a = EnumLevel::B as u8;         // COMPILES FINE downstream
let b = VariantLevel::First as u8;  // error[E0606]: casting `VariantLevel` as `u8` is invalid
                                    //   = note: cannot cast an enum with a non-exhaustive variant
                                    //           when it's defined in another crate
```
Enum-level `#[non_exhaustive]` does **not** block `as`. Only a `#[non_exhaustive]` *variant* does (and it also makes the variant unconstructible: `error[E0603]: unit variant First is private`). Authoritative text is in [the Rust Reference, non_exhaustive](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/attributes/type_system.html), not the cargo page.

**Does serde's derive work on a `#[non_exhaustive]` struct? Yes — unconditionally.** The derive expands inside the defining crate where the attribute is inert. Verified end-to-end:

```rust
#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize, JsonSchema, Debug, Default)]
#[non_exhaustive]
#[serde(rename_all = "snake_case")]
pub struct Wisp { pub id: String, #[serde(default, skip_serializing_if="Option::is_none")] pub note: Option<String> }
```
```
D roundtrip: Wisp { id: "x", note: None }     // from {"id":"x","note":null,"future_field":42}
```
Deserialize works, `Default` works, unknown fields ignored, and downstream crates in `down` deserialize it fine too. Same for a `#[non_exhaustive]` enum. **There is no serde/non_exhaustive interaction to worry about.**

**Does adding a variant to a `#[non_exhaustive]` enum count as breaking?** No. [Cargo semver reference](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/semver.html#enum-variant-new), verbatim:

> **Major: adding new enum variants (without `non_exhaustive`)** — It is a breaking change to add a new enum variant **if the enum does not use the `#[non_exhaustive]` attribute.**
> Mitigation strategies: When introducing the enum, mark it as `#[non_exhaustive]` to force users to use wildcard patterns to catch new variants.

That is the whole reason `cargo_metadata` carries **25 `#[non_exhaustive]` attributes** on its wire structs and **zero** `deny_unknown_fields`.

## 1e. Ordered enum serialized as a JSON string

Straightforward — `Ord` derives from declaration order, `Serialize` derives a plain string. Verified:

```rust
#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize, JsonSchema, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord)]
#[serde(rename_all = "snake_case")]
pub enum Severity { Info, Warning, Error }
```
```
F Severity schema = {"$schema":"...","title":"Severity","type":"string","enum":["info","warning","error"]}
F ord: true          // Severity::Info < Severity::Error
F json: "warning"
```

**Pitfalls, in order of how badly they bite:**

1. **Ordering is declaration order, and it is invisible in the wire format.** Reordering variants "for readability" silently inverts comparisons. Adding a severity in the middle silently shifts everything after it. Nothing in the JSON, the schema, or any test that only round-trips will catch this. **Mitigation:** assign explicit discriminants (`Info = 10, Warning = 20, Error = 30`) so the intent is in the source, add gaps so insertion doesn't require renumbering, and write a test that asserts the full sorted order.
2. **Ordering is lexically unrelated to the string.** `"error" < "info" < "warning"` alphabetically, but `Info < Warning < Error` semantically. Anything that sorts the JSON side (a jq pipeline, a JS consumer, a sorted map keyed by the string) gets a *different* order than Rust. If ordering must survive the wire, either serialize an integer or publish the ranking in the contract doc.
3. **`#[non_exhaustive]` blocks exhaustive `match` but not `as`** (see 1d) — so `Severity::Error as u8` still works downstream and quietly bakes your discriminants into consumer code. If you don't want that, add `#[non_exhaustive]` to a variant, or expose an explicit `fn rank(&self) -> u8`.
4. **A `#[serde(other)]` fallback variant has to live somewhere in the `Ord` sequence** and there is no good answer — `Unknown` sorts either below `Info` or above `Error`, both wrong. If the enum is both ordered *and* open, make it a struct with a private `u8` rank plus a `&'static str`, or accept that `Unknown` sorts last and document it.
5. `rename_all` is part of the wire contract but invisible to `Ord`. Changing it is a silent, total wire break that no Rust-side test detects.

**Bonus finding — open-enum idioms, since this is the actual forward-compat risk.** Every surveyed crate made its wire enums open; **a bare derived enum with no fallback arm is the one thing none of them ship on a wire type.** Four idioms, all verified:

```rust
// (a) #[serde(other)] on a PLAIN externally-tagged unit enum.
// serde's docs say "only allowed inside an internally or adjacently tagged enum" — that is WRONG,
// it works on a bare unit-only enum. But the round-trip is LOSSY.
#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize, JsonSchema, Debug)]
#[serde(rename_all = "snake_case")]
enum Algo { Sha256, Blake3, #[serde(other)] Unknown }
```
```
other de known   = Ok(Sha256)
other de unknown = Ok(Unknown)              // "md5" -> Unknown
other ser        = Ok("\"unknown\"")        // <-- "md5" became "unknown". Data destroyed.
Algo schema      = {"type":"string","enum":["sha256","blake3","unknown"]}
```

```rust
// (b) untagged String fallback (cargo_metadata TargetKind style) — LOSSLESS.
#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize, JsonSchema, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord)]
#[serde(rename_all = "snake_case")]
#[non_exhaustive]
enum Kind2 { Bin, Lib, #[serde(untagged)] Unknown(String) }
```
```
untagged unknown = Ok(Unknown("cdylib"))
untagged ser     = Ok("\"cdylib\"")         // original preserved
Kind2 schema     = {"anyOf":[{"type":"string","enum":["bin","lib"]},{"type":"string"}]}
ord: [Bin, Lib, Unknown("z")]
```

**Take (b), not (a), for anything a middle-tier repo forwards.** (a) is a data-destroying proxy: repo B reading and re-emitting a document from repo C on a newer version rewrites `"md5"` to `"unknown"`. The cost of (b) is that the published schema degrades to "any string" (`anyOf` with a bare `{"type":"string"}`) — the enumeration becomes a hint, not a constraint. If you need the schema to stay tight, keep the closed enum and add a `pattern`/`enum` via `#[schemars(extend(...))]`, accepting that the schema is stricter than the parser.

Two more from the survey, both worth stealing:

```rust
// (c) oci-spec-rs: hand-written Serialize/Deserialize through String — deserialization CANNOT fail.
impl<'de> Deserialize<'de> for MediaType {
    fn deserialize<D>(deserializer: D) -> Result<Self, D::Error> where D: Deserializer<'de> {
        let media_type = String::deserialize(deserializer)?;
        Ok(media_type.as_str().into())   // infallible; unknown -> Other(..)
    }
}
```
```rust
// (d) oci-spec-rs DigestAlgorithm — belt AND braces, with the rationale in the doc comment.
/// Other digest algorithms may be added in the future, so this structure is marked as non-exhaustive.
#[non_exhaustive]
pub enum DigestAlgorithm { Sha256, Sha384, Sha512, Other(Box<str>) }
```

And `lsp-types` sidesteps the whole question by not using Rust enums on the wire at all — `#[serde(transparent)] pub struct SymbolKind(i32);` plus associated consts, so `SymbolKind(99)` deserializes cleanly. Their own source carries a TODO ([`src/lib.rs:740`](https://github.com/gluon-lang/lsp-types)) explaining they *wanted* internally-tagged + `#[serde(other)]` and fell back to `untagged` because of [serde#912](https://github.com/serde-rs/serde/issues/912).

# 2. schemars conventions

## 2a. Current version and what changed

**`schemars` 1.2.2** (published 2026-07-27) is current stable. 1.0.0 landed **2025-06-23**. `edition = "2021"`, `rust-version = "1.74"`. **0.8 is legacy** — migrate. Sources: [crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/schemars), [CHANGELOG](https://github.com/GREsau/schemars/blob/master/CHANGELOG.md), [migration guide](https://graham.cool/schemars/migrating/).

What changed for derive users (from the [migration guide](https://graham.cool/schemars/migrating/)):

1. **`Schema` is now a thin wrapper around `serde_json::Value`**, not a struct-per-keyword. `schemars::schema::{SchemaObject, InstanceType, ObjectValidation, ...}` are **all gone**; `RootSchema` is gone (functions return `Schema`). New `json_schema!(...)` macro, works like `serde_json::json!`. This is the big one and it makes hand-written impls dramatically nicer.
2. **`visit::Visitor` → `transform::Transform`.** `SchemaSettings::visitors` → `.transforms`, `with_visitor` → `with_transform`, `GenVisitor` → `GenTransform`. `Transform` is implemented for any `fn(&mut Schema)`, so you can pass a bare function. `RecursiveTransform` newtype adapts a non-recursive one.
3. **Optional deps are version-suffixed**: `chrono` → `chrono04`, `url` → `url2`, `uuid` → `uuid1`, `semver` → `semver1`, etc. `enumset`/`indexmap`/`uuid08`/`arrayvec05`/`bigdecimal03` removed.
4. **`#[schemars(example = ...)]` changed meaning** — it now takes a *value* (anything `Serialize`), not a function-name string. Single-word string literals and paths are **deliberately rejected** to stop old code silently changing meaning. Use `example = my_fn()` for the old behavior, or `example = &"my_fn"` for a literal.
5. `#[validate(...)]` handling realigned to Validator 0.18; `#[garde(...)]` now supported; `regex = "..."` name-value syntax removed in favor of `regex(pattern = ...)`.
6. New: `#[schemars(!attr)]` "unsets" a serde attribute so schemars ignores it. New `#[schemars(extend(...))]`, `#[schemars(transform = ...)]`, `#[schemars(inline)]`.
7. 1.1.0 added `#[must_use]` to side-effect-free public fns — **relevant to you**, since your workspace denies on lints; a `schema_for!` result you drop now warns.
8. `gen` module and `SchemaSettings::option_nullable`/`option_add_null_type` removed in rc.2.

Note `Schema` wraps `serde_json::Value`, so **`serde_json` is a public dependency of `schemars`**, and `schemars` is a public dependency of `wisp-contracts` the moment a `JsonSchema` impl appears in your public API.

## 2b. Title, description, `$schema`, `$id`

All verified in one run:

```rust
/// A Wisp artifact envelope.
///
/// Second paragraph becomes part of the description.
#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize, JsonSchema)]
#[serde(rename_all = "snake_case")]
#[schemars(
    extend("$id" = "https://wisp.dev/schemas/envelope-v1.json"),
    extend("additionalProperties" = true),
)]
#[non_exhaustive]
pub struct Envelope {
    /// Schema version. Producers MUST set this.
    pub version: u32,
}
```
```json
{
  "$id": "https://wisp.dev/schemas/envelope-v1.json",
  "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
  "title": "Envelope",
  "description": "A Wisp artifact envelope.\n\nSecond paragraph becomes part of the description.",
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "version": { "description": "Schema version. Producers MUST set this.", "type": "integer", "format": "uint32", "minimum": 0 }
  },
  "additionalProperties": true,
  "required": ["version"]
}
```

- **description** — doc comments, automatically, on containers *and* fields. No attribute needed.
- **title** — defaults to the type name. Override with `#[schemars(title = "...")]`, or with an ATX markdown heading as the doc comment's first line: `/// # Digest` sets `title: "Digest"` and the rest becomes the description (verified). Explicit `#[schemars(title=)]`/`#[schemars(description=)]` win over doc comments.
- **`$id`** — no dedicated attribute; use `#[schemars(extend("$id" = "..."))]`. `extend` takes any `Serialize` value or a JSON literal, can repeat, keys must be unique.
- **`$schema`** — comes from `SchemaSettings::meta_schema`, injected at the root by `root_schema_for`. Verified all three modes:

```rust
schema_for!(Envelope)                                    // -> "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema"
SchemaSettings::draft07().into_generator()
    .root_schema_for::<Envelope>()                       // -> "$schema": "http://json-schema.org/draft-07/schema#"
SchemaSettings::draft2020_12().with(|s| s.meta_schema = None)
    .into_generator().root_schema_for::<Envelope>()      // -> no "$schema" key at all
```

Available: `draft07()`, `draft2019_09()`, `draft2020_12()` (the default), `openapi3()` — [`schemars/src/generate.rs:78-124`](https://github.com/GREsau/schemars/blob/master/schemars/src/generate.rs). **For MCP `outputSchema`, set `meta_schema = None`** — MCP embeds the schema object inside a tool descriptor, and a stray `$schema` is at best noise and at worst rejected by strict clients.

## 2c. The optional-feature gotcha — confirmed, and it is a hard compile error

**The gotcha:** `#[cfg_attr(feature = "schemars", derive(JsonSchema))]` correctly gates the *derive*, but a bare `#[schemars(...)]` **helper attribute** is only registered by that derive. With the feature off, the attribute has no registrar and the crate does not build:

```rust
#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[cfg_attr(feature = "schemars", derive(schemars::JsonSchema))]
pub struct Bad {
    #[schemars(regex(pattern = r"^x$"))]   // <-- BOOM with default features
    pub a: String,
}
```
```
error: cannot find attribute `schemars` in this scope
  --> src/lib.rs:14:7
   |
14 |     #[schemars(regex(pattern = r"^x$"))]
   |       ^^^^^^^^
```

**Every** `#[schemars(...)]` attribute must be wrapped too:

```rust
#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[cfg_attr(feature = "schemars", derive(schemars::JsonSchema))]
pub struct Fixed {
    #[cfg_attr(feature = "schemars", schemars(regex(pattern = r"^x$")))]
    pub a: String,
}
```
Verified: builds clean both with and without `--features schemars`. **CI must build both ways** — `cargo hack --each-feature` or at minimum a bare `cargo check` plus `cargo check --all-features`. A default-on feature hides this from every developer until an external consumer turns it off.

Bare `#[serde(...)]` attributes are fine unwrapped — schemars *reads* serde attributes, so `rename_all`, `tag`, `deny_unknown_fields`, `transparent`, `skip`, `default`, `flatten`, `with`, `from`/`try_from`/`into`, `bound` all carry over automatically ([attributes doc](https://graham.cool/schemars/deriving/attributes/)). You only need `#[schemars(...)]` to *diverge* from serde.

Cargo wiring:

```toml
[dependencies]
schemars = { version = "1", optional = true }   # keep default features: derive + std

[features]
schemars = ["dep:schemars"]   # dep: prefix, so the implicit feature isn't created
```

Two things to know about `dep:`: without it, Cargo auto-creates a feature named after the optional dep, and per the [semver reference](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/semver.html#cargo-remove-opt-dep), *"Removing an optional dependency can break a project using your library because another project may be enabling that dependency via Cargo features"* — `dep:` suppresses the implicit feature and keeps that escape hatch. Also: do **not** add `default-features = false` to the `schemars` dep unless you mean it — that turns off `derive` (the macro lives behind it) and `std`.

**Feature-unification hazards, two real ones:**

1. **`schemars/preserve_order` is `["serde_json/preserve_order"]`** ([Cargo.toml](https://github.com/GREsau/schemars/blob/master/schemars/Cargo.toml)). Cargo features are unioned graph-wide, so *any* crate in *any* of your four repos enabling it flips `serde_json::Map` from `BTreeMap` to `IndexMap` **for the entire build**. That silently changes JSON key ordering in every canonical artifact you write — which, given your atomic-write/canonical-artifact invariant, means digests change without a source change. Pin this down: if you canonicalize, either enable `preserve_order` deliberately and everywhere, or forbid it and assert sorted-key output in a test.
2. Standard serde/no_std unification, [serde.rs/no-std.html](https://serde.rs/no-std.html): *"Cargo features are unioned together across your entire dependency graph. That means if any other crate you depend on has not opted out of Serde's default features, you will build Serde with the `std` feature enabled whether or not your direct dependency on Serde has `default-features = false`."* Your `no_std` is aspirational unless the whole graph cooperates.

Also relevant to your `unwrap_used`/`expect_used = deny` lints: schemars' own migration examples use `.expect(...)`. Any `Schema` manipulation you copy from the guide needs rewriting.

## 2d. Emitting `{"type":"string","pattern":"..."}` for a newtype — three working routes

**All three verified. Pick route 1.**

### Route 1 — manual `JsonSchema` impl with `json_schema!` (recommended)

```rust
use schemars::{JsonSchema, Schema, SchemaGenerator, json_schema};
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
use std::borrow::Cow;

pub const DIGEST_PATTERN: &str = r"^(sha256|blake3):[a-f0-9]{64}$";

#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize, Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord, Hash)]
#[serde(transparent)]
pub struct Digest(String);

impl JsonSchema for Digest {
    fn schema_name() -> Cow<'static, str> { "Digest".into() }
    fn schema_id() -> Cow<'static, str> { "wisp_contracts::Digest".into() }
    fn inline_schema() -> bool { false }   // false => referenced via $ref in $defs
    fn json_schema(_generator: &mut SchemaGenerator) -> Schema {
        json_schema!({
            "type": "string",
            "pattern": DIGEST_PATTERN,
            "title": "Digest",
            "description": "Content digest, `<algo>:<hex>`.",
        })
    }
}
```
```json
{
  "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
  "title": "Digest",
  "description": "Content digest, `<algo>:<hex>`.",
  "type": "string",
  "pattern": "^(sha256|blake3):[a-f0-9]{64}$"
}
```

Why this one: the regex is a `const` you can **share with the `FromStr` validator**, so the published schema and the parser cannot drift — which is the entire point of a vocabulary crate. It also needs no `#[cfg_attr]` gymnastics on fields, and `schema_id` gives you a stable `$ref` key independent of the display name. The whole impl goes behind `#[cfg(feature = "schemars")]`.

Trait signature confirmed from [`schemars/src/lib.rs`](https://github.com/GREsau/schemars/blob/master/schemars/src/lib.rs): `inline_schema()` (default `false`), `schema_name() -> Cow<'static, str>` (required), `schema_id()` (defaults to `schema_name`), `json_schema(&mut SchemaGenerator) -> Schema` (required). Note this is the 1.x shape — 0.8's was `is_referenceable()` + `schema_name() -> String` + `json_schema(&mut gen) -> schema::Schema`.

### Route 2 — derive + `regex(pattern = ...)` on the inner field

```rust
#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize, JsonSchema)]
#[serde(transparent)]
pub struct DigestB(#[schemars(regex(pattern = r"^(sha256|blake3):[a-f0-9]{64}$"))] String);
```
```json
{"$schema":"...","title":"DigestB","type":"string","pattern":"^(sha256|blake3):[a-f0-9]{64}$"}
```
Works. Use a `r"raw string"` so `\d`/`\.` aren't eaten as Rust escapes — the [docs say so explicitly](https://graham.cool/schemars/deriving/attributes/). `#[schemars(pattern(r"..."))]` (Garde style) is equivalent. `path = ...` is **not** allowed inside a `schemars` attribute; `regex(pattern = *static_regex)` is, if you want to point at a compiled `Regex`.

### Route 3 — derive + container-level `extend`

```rust
#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize, JsonSchema)]
#[serde(transparent)]
#[schemars(extend("pattern" = r"^(sha256|blake3):[a-f0-9]{64}$"))]
pub struct DigestC(String);
```
```json
{"$schema":"...","title":"DigestC","type":"string","pattern":"^(sha256|blake3):[a-f0-9]{64}$"}
```
Identical output, and `extend` is the general escape hatch for any keyword schemars has no attribute for (`$id`, `$comment`, `examples`, `format`, `deprecated`, `unevaluatedProperties`, …).

**Both 2 and 3 need `#[cfg_attr(feature = "schemars", ...)]` wrapping** per §2c. Route 1 doesn't, because the whole `impl` block is `#[cfg]`'d.

**On `schemars(with = ...)`:** it exists and works on containers, variants, and fields, but it must name **an actual type implementing `JsonSchema`**, not a module path like serde's `with`. Generic params must be fully spelled: `with = "Vec::<i32>"` works, `with = "Vec"` and `with = "Vec::<_>"` do not. `#[schemars(with = "String")]` is the right move for a `FromStr` newtype whose inner representation isn't a `String` (e.g. `Digest([u8; 32])` serialized via `serialize_with`) — but you'd then still need `extend`/`regex` for the pattern, so route 1 remains simpler.

**`schema_with`:** `#[schemars(schema_with = "some::function")]` is field/variant-only (not containers) and the function is `fn(&mut schemars::SchemaGenerator) -> Schema`. Since 1.0.0-alpha.22 it accepts generics: `schema_with = "func::<T>"`. Fine for one-off fields; for a named newtype used across four repos, the trait impl is the right home.

# 3. Cargo semver reference — the rules that matter for a vocabulary crate

Source: <https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/semver.html>. The classification vocabulary is defined up front:

> **Major change**: a change that requires a major SemVer bump. **Minor change**: a change that requires only a minor SemVer bump. **Possibly-breaking change**: a change that some projects may consider major and others consider minor.

And the crucial `0.x` note — **directly relevant, since your workspace is at `version = "0.0.0"`**:

> This guide uses the terms "major" and "minor" assuming this relates to a "1.0.0" release or later. Initial development releases starting with "0.y.z" can treat changes in "y" as a major release, and "z" as a minor release. **"0.0.z" releases are always major changes.** This is because Cargo uses the convention that only changes in the left-most non-zero component are considered incompatible.

## The rules, verbatim

**Adding an enum variant** — [`enum-variant-new`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/semver.html#enum-variant-new):
> **Major: adding new enum variants (without `non_exhaustive`)**
> It is a breaking change to add a new enum variant if the enum does not use the `#[non_exhaustive]` attribute.
> *Mitigation strategies:* When introducing the enum, mark it as `#[non_exhaustive]` to force users to use wildcard patterns to catch new variants.

Corollary, unstated but implied and universally relied on: **adding a variant to an already-`#[non_exhaustive]` enum is minor.**

**Adding fields to an enum variant** — separately major:
> **Major: adding new fields to an enum variant.** It is a breaking change to add new fields to an enum variant because all fields are public, and constructors and matching will fail to compile.
> *Mitigation:* mark the variant as `non_exhaustive`, **or** use an explicit struct as a value, where you can have control over the field visibility.

That second mitigation is the shape to prefer for a vocabulary crate — `Variant1(Foo)` where `Foo` is a `#[non_exhaustive] pub struct` — because it keeps the payload independently versionable.

**Adding a struct field** — two separate major rules:
> **Major: adding a public field when no private field exists.** When a public field is added to a struct that has all public fields, this will break any code that attempts to construct it with a struct literal. `let x = Foo { f1: 123 }; // Error: missing field f2`
> **Major: adding a private struct field when all current fields are public.** `let x = Foo { f1: 123 }; // Error: cannot construct Foo`
> *Mitigation (both):* Do not add new fields to all-public field structs. **Mark structs as `#[non_exhaustive]` when first introducing a struct** to prevent users from using struct literal syntax, and instead provide a constructor method and/or `Default` implementation.

> **Minor: adding or removing private fields when at least one already exists.** This is safe because existing code cannot use a struct literal to construct it, nor exhaustively match its contents. Note that for tuple structs, this is a major change if the tuple contains public fields, and the addition or removal of a private field changes the index of any public field.

Two mechanisms achieve the same thing, and the surveyed crates split on which: `cargo_metadata` puts `#[non_exhaustive]` on 25 all-public wire structs; `oci-spec-rs` uses private fields + `Getters`/`Builder` derives. Pick one and apply it uniformly.

**`non_exhaustive` on/off** — [`attr-adding-non-exhaustive`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/semver.html#attr-adding-non-exhaustive):
> **Major: adding `non_exhaustive` to an existing enum, variant, or struct with no private fields.**
> Making items `#[non_exhaustive]` changes how they may be used outside the crate where they are defined:
> - Non-exhaustive structs and enum variants cannot be constructed using struct literal syntax, **including functional update syntax**.
> - Pattern matching on non-exhaustive structs requires `..` and matching on enums does not count towards exhaustiveness.
> - Casting enum variants to their discriminant with `as` is not allowed.
> - Structs with private fields cannot be constructed using struct literal syntax regardless of whether `#[non_exhaustive]` is used. **Adding `#[non_exhaustive]` to such a struct is not a breaking change.**
> *Mitigation:* Mark structs, enums, and enum variants as `#[non_exhaustive]` **when first introducing them**, rather than adding `#[non_exhaustive]` later on.

(The `as` bullet is imprecise — see §1d for the verified enum-level vs variant-level distinction.)

**This is the single highest-leverage decision for `wisp-contracts`, and it is a one-way door.** Adding it later is major; adding it now is free. Do it now, on everything, before v1.

**Removing `non_exhaustive`** is not listed — it is `Minor: adding new public items`-shaped (it only relaxes), though it permanently forfeits the future ability to add fields.

**Adding a trait impl.** There is **no rule stating "adding a trait impl is major"** — it falls under [`item-new`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/semver.html#item-new):
> **Minor: adding new public items.** Adding new, public items is a minor change.
> Note that in some rare cases this can be a breaking change due to glob imports. For example, if you add a new trait, and a project has used a glob import that brings that trait into scope, and the new trait introduces an associated item that conflicts with any types it is implemented on, this can cause a compile-time error due to the ambiguity. **This is not considered a major change because conventionally glob imports are a known forwards-compatibility hazard.**

The adjacent rule you *do* need to respect:
> **Possibly-breaking change: adding any inherent items.** Usually adding inherent items to an implementation should be safe because inherent items take priority over trait items. However, in some cases the collision can cause problems if the name is the same as an implemented trait item with a different signature. Note that if the signatures match, there would not be a compile-time error, but **possibly a silent change in runtime behavior**.

Practical reading for a vocabulary crate: `impl Serialize/Deserialize/JsonSchema/Display/FromStr/Ord for YourType` is **minor**. Adding an inherent method named like a trait method your consumers already call is **possibly-breaking**. Adding a *trait* is minor-with-a-glob-caveat. Adding a blanket impl is the dangerous one — it can collide with a downstream impl and is effectively unremovable.

**Adding a public dependency's type to a public signature.** The reference has **no rule for this** — I grepped the full page. What it does say:
> **Minor: adding dependencies.** It is usually safe to add new dependencies, as long as the new dependency does not introduce new requirements that result in a breaking change.

The actual mechanic, which you must reason about yourself: once `pub fn f() -> schemars::Schema` (or `-> camino::Utf8PathBuf`) is in your public API, that dependency is *public*. A **major bump of that dependency becomes a major bump of `wisp-contracts`**, because Cargo will link two incompatible copies and the consumer gets `expected schemars::Schema, found schemars::Schema`. Across four repos this is the classic diamond that pins everyone. Cargo has an **unstable** `public-dependency` feature (["Allows dependencies to be classified as either public or private"](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/unstable.html#public-dependency)) that will lint this; it is not stable, so today the discipline is manual.

For a vocabulary crate the concrete rule is: **keep public dependencies to serde and (feature-gated) schemars, and nothing else.** Every additional type from a third-party crate in a public signature — `camino::Utf8PathBuf`, `url::Url`, `uuid::Uuid`, `jiff::Timestamp` — is a semver liability shared by all four repos. Own the newtype, expose `FromStr`/`Display`/`AsRef<str>`, and let *consumers* convert. Note `schemars`' own `Schema` publicly wraps `serde_json::Value`, so enabling the schemars feature transitively makes `serde_json` public too.

Related and worth knowing:
> **Minor: adding a new Cargo feature.** **Major: removing a Cargo feature.** **Possibly-breaking: removing an optional dependency** — Removing an optional dependency can break a project using your library because another project may be enabling that dependency via Cargo features... This problem can be avoided by using the `dep:` syntax in the `[features]` table, which disables this implicit feature.

**MSRV bumps** — [`env-new-rust`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/semver.html#env-new-rust):
> **Possibly-breaking: changing the minimum version of Rust required.**
> Introducing the use of new features in a new release of Rust can break projects that are using older versions of Rust.
> **It is generally recommended to treat this as a minor change, rather than as a major change**, for various reasons. It is usually relatively easy to update to a newer version of Rust. Rust also has a rapid 6-week release cycle, and some projects will provide compatibility within a window of releases. Just keep in mind that some large projects may not be able to update their Rust toolchain rapidly.
> *Mitigation:* Document your package's minimum-supported Rust version by setting `package.rust-version`, allowing Cargo's dependency resolution to attempt to select older versions of your package when needed. Use Cargo features to make the new features opt-in. Provide a large window of support for older releases.

You already set `rust-version = "1.96"`. Note that `edition = "2024"` **hard-floors you at 1.85**, so a vocabulary crate meant for wide reuse might sensibly stay on edition 2021 — schemars itself does (`edition = "2021"`, `rust-version = "1.74"`) for exactly this reason. Also note that `resolver = "3"` requires 1.84+.

**And the one that decides §4 for you** — [`attr-no-std-to-std`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/semver.html#attr-no-std-to-std):
> **Major: switching from `no_std` support to requiring `std`.** If your library specifically supports a `no_std` environment, it is a breaking change to make a new release that requires `std`.
> *Mitigation:* A common idiom to avoid this is to include a `std` Cargo feature that optionally enables `std` support, and when the feature is off, the library can be used in a `no_std` environment.

**`no_std` is a one-way commitment.** Ship it and you cannot un-ship it without a major bump.

# 4. `no_std` for a small vocabulary crate

## What serde needs

[serde.rs/no-std.html](https://serde.rs/no-std.html), verbatim:

> The serde crate has a Cargo feature named "std" that is enabled by default. In order to use Serde in a `no_std` context this feature needs to be disabled.
> **Be aware that Cargo features are unioned together across your entire dependency graph.** That means if any other crate you depend on has not opted out of Serde's default features, you will build Serde with the `std` feature enabled whether or not your direct dependency on Serde has `default-features = false`.
> Opting out of the "std" feature of Serde removes support for any standard library data structures that involve heap memory allocation, including `String` and `Vec<T>`. It also removes some features of `derive(Deserialize)` **including untagged enums**. You can opt back in to these impls by enabling the "alloc" Cargo feature.

```toml
serde      = { version = "1", default-features = false, features = ["alloc", "derive"] }
serde_json = { version = "1", default-features = false, features = ["alloc"] }
```

`#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]` itself works identically in `no_std`. What you lose without `alloc`: `String`, `Vec<T>`, untagged enums, **and internally- and adjacently-tagged enums** ([enum-representations](https://serde.rs/enum-representations.html): *"All enum representations work in no-std projects, but externally tagged is the only one that works in no-alloc projects"*). With `alloc` you get all of them back. Since a JSON vocabulary crate is made of `String`s, **you want `no_std + alloc`, never no-alloc** — and that means you keep every tagging option.

## Does schemars support `no_std`? Yes.

Directly from [`schemars/src/lib.rs`](https://github.com/GREsau/schemars/blob/master/schemars/src/lib.rs):
```rust
#![forbid(unsafe_code)]
#![no_std]

extern crate alloc;
#[cfg(feature = "std")]
extern crate std;
```
And [`schemars/Cargo.toml`](https://github.com/GREsau/schemars/blob/master/schemars/Cargo.toml):
```toml
categories = ["encoding", "no-std"]
[dependencies]
serde      = { version = "1.0.194", default-features = false, features = ["alloc"] }
serde_json = { version = "1.0.127", default-features = false, features = ["alloc"] }
[features]
default = ["derive", "std"]
# Provide impls for common standard library types like `HashMap<K, V>`.
# Requires a dependency on the Rust standard library.
std = []
derive = ["schemars_derive"]
```

So `schemars = { version = "1", default-features = false, features = ["derive"] }` gives you `no_std + alloc` schemars. **The crate itself is `#![no_std]` unconditionally** — `std` only adds impls for `HashMap`/`HashSet`/`OsString`/`PathBuf`/etc. Caveat: 1.0.1 was a patch fixing *"Deriving `JsonSchema` with `no_std` broken due to `std::borrow::ToOwned` trait not being in scope"* — the path is supported but not as heavily trodden as `std`.

## What concretely becomes impossible without `std`

**`FromStr` — nothing breaks.** `core::str::FromStr` is in `core`. Fully usable.

**`Display` — nothing breaks.** `core::fmt::Display` is in `core`. `format!`/`ToString` need `alloc`, which you have.

**`std::error::Error` — this is the interesting one, and it is a solved problem.** `core::error` was **stabilized in Rust 1.81.0, released 2024-09-05**, per the [official release notes](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/master/RELEASES.md) (Version 1.81.0, Stabilized APIs: `core::error`). Your `rust-version = "1.96"` and edition-2024 floor of 1.85 both sit comfortably above it, so `impl core::error::Error for DigestParseError {}` just works with no `std` and no feature gate.

**But your error crate might not follow.** `thiserror` 2.x generates `std::error::Error` impls by default and needs `default-features = false` for the `core::error::Error` path — check that before assuming. `miette` (in your workspace deps) is unambiguously `std`-only, but it belongs in `wisp-cli`, not in a vocabulary crate.

**The things that genuinely disappear**, and whether a vocabulary crate cares:

| Lost without `std` | Matters for `wisp-contracts`? |
| :-- | :-- |
| `HashMap` / `HashSet` | No — use `BTreeMap`/`BTreeSet`, which you want anyway for **deterministic JSON key order** given your canonical-artifact/atomic-write invariant |
| `Path`, `PathBuf`, `OsString`, `camino::Utf8PathBuf` | **Yes, decisively** — if the vocabulary carries paths |
| `std::time::SystemTime`, `Instant` | Yes if it carries timestamps (mitigable: store an `i64` epoch or an RFC-3339 `String`) |
| `std::io`, filesystem, network | No — a vocabulary crate does no I/O |
| `std::error::Error` | **No** — `core::error::Error` since 1.81 |
| Default RNG, `std::process` | No |

## The decision

**Recommendation: skip `no_std` unless you have a named embedded/wasm-no-std consumer today.**

The case *against*, concretely:

1. **The gain is near zero for your stated consumers.** Four repos plus an MCP server are all hosted `std` targets. `wasm32-unknown-unknown` and `wasm32-wasip1` both have full `std`.
2. **The graph will not cooperate.** Feature unification means `serde/std` gets turned on by anything else in the tree; `jsonschema` 0.53, `miette`, `clap`, and `camino` are all `std`-only. Your `no_std` would be nominal, unverified in every real build, and would rot the first time nobody runs the `--no-default-features` job. Verifying it honestly requires a dedicated `cargo build --target thumbv7em-none-eabi --no-default-features` CI job — real recurring cost.
3. **It constrains the type design permanently.** No `Utf8PathBuf` in the vocabulary, no `SystemTime`, `BTreeMap` everywhere.
4. **`no_std` is a one-way door** per §3: *"Major: switching from `no_std` support to requiring `std`."* Advertise it and you owe a major bump to walk it back.

The case *for*: it costs almost nothing **structurally** if you do it now, and everything else in your design already points that way — `unsafe_code = "forbid"` matches schemars' own posture, `BTreeMap` is right for canonical output regardless, `core::error::Error` is free at 1.81+, and `alloc`-gated serde loses you no tagging representation.

**The middle path, which is what I'd actually do:** declare a `std` feature in `default`, write the crate so it *would* compile without it (`use core::fmt`, `core::str::FromStr`, `core::error::Error`, `BTreeMap` over `HashMap`, no `Path` in the vocabulary), and **do not advertise `no_std` support or add a CI target for it.** You keep the discipline and the option; you take on neither the CI cost nor the semver commitment. If a `no_std` consumer ever shows up, the door is a `#![cfg_attr(not(feature = "std"), no_std)]` line and a CI job away — and per the semver reference, *adding* `no_std` support is only a minor change.

## Condensed recommendations for `wisp-contracts`

| Decision | Call | Why |
| :-- | :-- | :-- |
| Casting | `snake_case` (no `rename_all`) if Rust-native; `camelCase` only if mirroring an external spec | cargo/rustc precedent; zero rename drift |
| `deny_unknown_fields` | **Never on wire types.** Config only. | 0/5 surveyed crates use it; serde's default is already right; [aws#750](https://github.com/aws/aws-lambda-rust-runtime/issues/750) |
| `#[non_exhaustive]` | **On every public struct and enum, from day one** | Adding it later is major; it's what makes field/variant addition minor |
| Enum tagging | Adjacent (`tag`+`content`) or internal; **never untagged** for a versioned envelope | Internal breaks on tuple/primitive payloads (runtime!) and all binary formats |
| Open enums | `#[serde(untagged)] Unknown(String)`, not `#[serde(other)]` | `other` destroys the original string on re-serialize — fatal for a forwarding middle tier |
| `flatten` | Avoid entirely in the vocabulary | Broken with `deny_unknown_fields` in ways that compile and silently misbehave |
| Ordering | Explicit gapped discriminants + a test asserting full sorted order | Declaration-order `Ord` is invisible in JSON and in the schema |
| schemars | 1.2.x, optional dep via `dep:`, **wrap every `#[schemars(...)]` in `cfg_attr`**, CI both ways | `error: cannot find attribute schemars in this scope` |
| Pattern newtypes | Manual `impl JsonSchema` + `json_schema!` + a shared `const` regex | Schema and `FromStr` validator provably cannot drift |
| MCP `outputSchema` | `SchemaSettings::draft2020_12().with(\|s\| s.meta_schema = None)` | Strip `$schema` for embedding |
| `preserve_order` | Decide explicitly and enforce workspace-wide | Graph-wide unification silently changes canonical JSON key order → digest churn |
| Public deps | serde + (gated) schemars only | Every other public type is a shared semver liability across four repos |
| `no_std` | Write as if; don't declare or CI it | Near-zero gain, real cost, one-way door |
| Contract doc | Copy rustc's sentence verbatim | *"Optional values may be `null`. New fields may be added. Enumerated fields... may add new values."* — makes leniency a specified feature, not an accident ([RFC 9413](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9413.html)) |
